articles.title: Justin Herbert: Basically Nothing
articles.deck: Corey Becker revisits the hype around Justin Herbert, the expectations that followed him, and what may come next for the Chargers.
articles.author: Corey Becker | JKSPORTSBOOK
articles.label: The Becker Report
articles.body:
52–54.

Sub .500.

Justin Herbert is bad. I don’t know if Brandon Staley infected him, and honestly, I don’t care.

He’s been terrible to watch, and I think it’s only a matter of time until he disappears into the QB room—if he’s lucky. I just have a hard time believing he’s that bad. Because let’s face the music: he’s actually that bad.

The media has spent the last few years throwing him into the top-five QB conversation. I didn’t see it then, and I definitely don’t see it now. The only difference is that I had enough discernment to know Brandon Staley was a moron of a head coach and Justin Herbert was a young QB. But Herbert is a veteran now, and the excuses have run out.

The market has started to adjust. Herbert finished 32nd on the player-merchandise list. And don’t say it doesn’t matter, because it does. Especially when you’re in LA—even if you should be in San Diego. Not his problem, but his problem if you know what I mean. And if you look at the 15 QBs ahead of him in sales, I probably wouldn’t take Herbert over any of them. Maybe Shedeur Sanders. Okay, definitely Shedeur Sanders. But still.

That puts Herbert close to 15th-best QB in the league, and that tracks with his sub-.500 record as a starter. It’s sad, really, because all the traits you’d want in a QB are there—except, you know, a winning mentality.

And he truly was a dual threat in college. College football counts sacks as rushing yards (don’t get me started), which hides how mobile he was at Oregon. Take those sacks out and he ran for 1,044 yards on 157 carries—6.6 yards per carry. He also scored 13 rushing touchdowns. That ability was real. He just hasn’t shown that same dual-threat side consistently in the NFL.

Perhaps Staley robbed him of that winning mentality. But where is the accountability? I don’t know. He seems like he lacks awareness of what’s unfolding—or crashing—around him. Blowing a 27-point playoff lead. Four picks in the wild-card game against Houston. A touchdown-less dud against the Pats last year. Yeah.

It’s time to move on. Honestly, I thought he’d be moved at the deadline. Maybe they’ll give him one last dance if they win the Jeremiah Smith sweepstakes, but I doubt it. There are a handful of teams that will need a QB in the offseason, and even if they could get Herbert for a bag of Cheetos, I don’t know if any front office would bite. The financial repercussions for the Chargers would be immense, so they’re probably better off waiting it out. Herbert does have a full no-trade clause, though, so he’d choose where he goes if a trade ever came up.

What sucks about this, if you’re a Chargers fan, is that you had every right to be excited in the early Herbert era. Even though he still shows flashes of greatness, they’re few and far between. Even a broken clock is right twice a day.

I feel for the fans. First the move. Now this.

The league was wrong about Justin Herbert, but only the Chargers will suffer for being wrong. It’s been a less-than-stellar career for a man whose ceiling truly was quite high.

articles.title: Fernando Mendoza: Remember Where You Heard It First
articles.deck: Some things don’t show up on film. Some players are destined for greatness long before the rest of the world realizes it. And sometimes, you just know.
articles.author: Corey Becker | JKSPORTSBOOK
articles.label: The Becker Report
articles.body:
For the last three weeks, I’ve been chasing a football card.

Not just any card. A Fernando Mendoza autographed card, numbered to just three copies.

I’ve searched listings, monitored prices, and watched cards disappear from the marketplace almost as quickly as they appeared.

Maybe it’s just hype. Maybe collectors are trying to capitalize on the next big thing. After all, speculation and sports collectibles have always gone hand in hand.

But something tells me there’s more to it.

Perhaps I’m not the only one who sees something special in this kid.

There’s a certain gravity to greatness. An inexplicable pull that draws people toward someone before they’ve accomplished enough to justify the attention.

Sometimes, the market recognizes something before the record books do.

And with Fernando Mendoza, I can’t shake the feeling that we’re watching the beginning of something extraordinary.

The Kid Who Made the Impossible Possible

Let’s consider what Fernando Mendoza has already accomplished.

The Indiana Hoosiers.

For generations, Indiana football was practically an afterthought. A program known more for its historical struggles than its victories. A university where basketball was religion and football was something to occupy the calendar until the hardwood came calling.

Then Curt Cignetti arrived.

And eventually, so did Fernando Mendoza.

What followed was one of the greatest stories in the history of college football.

Sixteen wins. Zero losses. A national championship.

Read that again.

The Indiana Hoosiers became national champions in football.

If somebody had written that screenplay five years ago, Hollywood might have rejected it for being too unrealistic.

But Mendoza didn’t just participate in that transformation. He became its leading man.

Under Cignetti, he developed into a Heisman Trophy winner and the face of a program that refused to accept its place in college football’s hierarchy.

Cignetti doesn’t strike me as somebody interested in motivational speeches without accountability. His philosophy is built around preparation, discipline, execution, and an almost obsessive commitment to winning.

And Mendoza thrived in that environment.

There’s something to be said about a young quarterback who doesn’t simply survive under a demanding coach but becomes the embodiment of everything that coach is trying to build.

Some quarterbacks are products of a system.

Others become the heartbeat of it.

I believe Mendoza was the latter.

A Baptism by Fire

Now imagine this.

You’ve just entered the NFL. You’ve yet to make your first professional start.

And your welcome-to-the-league moment comes against the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks.

Not exactly a soft landing.

Seattle, under Mike Macdonald, has built one of the most intimidating defenses in professional football. They’re physical, disciplined, fast, and capable of making experienced quarterbacks look like they’re trying to solve a Rubik’s Cube in the middle of a car accident.

They disguise coverages. They create confusion. And perhaps most importantly, they punish hesitation.

This isn’t a defense that simply waits for mistakes.

It manufactures them.

And that’s the opponent Fernando Mendoza gets for his first NFL start.

You couldn’t have scripted a more challenging introduction.

Yet, strangely enough, I love it.

Because if there’s one thing I’ve learned from watching sports, it’s that greatness rarely announces itself under comfortable circumstances.

Diamonds aren’t formed in the sunlight. They’re formed under pressure.

And if Mendoza is truly the player I believe he is, Sunday could give us our first glimpse of something special.

There’s another fascinating wrinkle to this matchup.

Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak spent last season helping Seattle win a Super Bowl as its offensive coordinator.

He knows the personnel. He understands the philosophy. He’s familiar with the very defense his rookie quarterback is preparing to face.

Whether that familiarity translates into an advantage remains to be seen.

But it certainly makes this matchup more interesting.

There’s Something About This Kid

I realize how ridiculous this might sound.

We’re talking about a rookie quarterback who hasn’t even made his first NFL start, and here I am discussing him as though his place in football history is already reserved.

But that’s the beauty of sports, isn’t it?

Sometimes, you see something before everyone else does.

People can debate his arm strength, his mobility, whether he benefited from Cignetti’s system, or whether his college success will translate to Sundays.

Others have questioned his personality.

I’ve seen people suggest that his relentless positivity, polished interviews, and seemingly unwavering humility feel almost too good to be true.

As though being a genuinely decent human being is somehow more suspicious than being an arrogant one.

I see it differently.

I see a young man who understands the weight of the opportunity he’s been given.

A young man who speaks with intention, carries himself with dignity, and seems genuinely grateful to be in the position he’s earned.

And above everything else?

I see a winner.

Not someone who merely enjoys winning.

Someone who expects it.

There’s a difference.

Tom Brady wasn’t the most physically gifted quarterback in his draft class. Drew Brees faced questions about whether his physical profile could translate into NFL success. Russell Wilson spent much of his early career proving that conventional evaluations don’t always account for the person underneath the helmet.

I’m not suggesting Mendoza plays like any of them.

But I am suggesting they share something that can’t be adequately measured with a stopwatch, a measuring tape, or a scouting grade.

Conviction.

The kind that doesn’t require announcing itself.

The kind that makes a fourth-quarter deficit feel like an inconvenience rather than a death sentence.

The kind that makes teammates believe they’re never truly out of a game.

And frankly, that’s something you can’t teach.

The First Chapter of Something Bigger

I’m not expecting perfection on Sunday.

There will probably be mistakes.

Seattle will disguise coverages Mendoza hasn’t seen before. The pocket will collapse faster than he’s accustomed to. There will be moments when the speed of the NFL becomes painfully apparent.

But I want to see what happens after those moments.

Does he hang his head?

Does he start playing cautiously?

Or does he respond the same way he did at Indiana, where pressure seemed less like an obstacle and more like an invitation?

Because the defining characteristic of great quarterbacks isn’t that they never get punched in the mouth.

It’s what happens when they do.

There’s a reason the best athletes in history seem almost immune to the psychological weight of the moment.

Michael Jordan wanted the final shot.

Tom Brady wanted the ball with two minutes remaining.

The greatest competitors don’t merely tolerate pressure.

They pursue it.

And something tells me Mendoza might be cut from that same cloth.

Seattle represents the storm.

Sunday, we’ll find out whether Mendoza knows how to navigate it.

I’m Planting My Flag

Here’s where I’m going to lose some people.

I’m not simply predicting Fernando Mendoza will be a good NFL quarterback.

I’m not suggesting he’ll eventually develop into a respectable starter who enjoys a decade-long career.

I’m going considerably further.

Fernando Mendoza is going to be a Hall of Famer.

And I believe he’s going to bring a Super Bowl championship to the Las Vegas Raiders.

There.

I said it.

Before his first NFL start.

Before he has an opportunity to establish himself against the best players on the planet.

Before the analysts, the pundits, and the talking heads have enough professional film to determine whether he’s the real deal.

I’m putting it in writing.

Could I be completely wrong?

Absolutely.

Maybe five years from now, somebody digs up this article and has a good laugh at my expense.

That’s fine.

I’ve been wrong before, and I’ll certainly be wrong again.

But I’ve also watched enough sports to understand that history has a peculiar way of revealing itself.

We spend years questioning greatness while it’s unfolding directly in front of us.

Then, once the championships have been won, the records have been broken, and the gold jackets have been fitted, we collectively convince ourselves that the outcome was inevitable.

Of course he was going to be great.

Of course he was going to win.

How could anyone have doubted him?

The signs were there all along.

Except they weren’t obvious to everyone.

Not at the time.

That’s what makes the people who recognized them early so interesting.

Remember Where You Heard It First

I think the Raiders beat the Seahawks on Sunday.

Call it a gut feeling. Call it an unreasonable amount of faith in a rookie quarterback. Call it whatever you want.

But I believe Fernando Mendoza is going to find a way.

More importantly, I believe Sunday’s game will eventually be remembered as the first chapter of a much bigger story.

A story that began with a seemingly impossible national championship at Indiana.

A story shaped by Curt Cignetti, strengthened by adversity, and carried forward by a young man who doesn’t seem particularly interested in accepting the limitations other people place on him.

Years from now, maybe we’ll look back on this moment differently.

Maybe we’ll remember the rookie who was thrown into the fire against the defending Super Bowl champions.

Maybe we’ll remember the quarterback who brought the Raiders back to the promised land.

Maybe we’ll remember the day we first began to understand what Fernando Mendoza was capable of becoming.

And hopefully, somewhere in my collection, I’ll have that one-of-three autographed card.

Not simply because it became valuable.

But because it’ll remind me of something I believed long before the rest of the world caught up.

Fernando Mendoza. Future Hall of Famer. Future Super Bowl champion.

And perhaps the most important part of all?

We knew it all along.

Remember where you heard it first.

articles.title: Why Build Another Sportsbook?
articles.deck: Corey Becker on independent sports coverage, the people behind JKSPORTSBOOK, and making a place worth visiting.
articles.author: Corey Becker
articles.label: Founding Perspective
articles.body:
The world doesn’t need another sportsbook. It doesn’t need another self-proclaimed expert with a microphone, a few opinions, and a Monday-morning explanation for why he was right. It doesn’t need another personality promising to lock in a winner, or another platform telling you what to think before you’ve had the chance to think for yourself.

So why the hell am I helping build one?

Because I keep coming back to the way we talk about sports—and the way we bet on them.

Somewhere between living and dying with the Buffalo Bills, developing an unhealthy fascination with tennis, and spending years studying betting markets, I realized the most interesting part of sports isn’t the box score. It’s the psychology, the narratives, the people willing to challenge conventional wisdom, and the stories that never make the headlines.

With betting now woven into how so many of us follow sports, I find myself wondering what deserves our attention, what holds up, and what we might be missing. I want to cover sports independently, follow the questions that actually interest me, and figure out what I think along the way.

And then there’s the craziness that brought me together with Josh King and got this whole thing started.

Josh and I may be cut from the same cloth, but you wouldn’t always know it from our personalities. He’s outspoken, unpredictable, and never seems too worried about what people think. Between his unsolicited rants about Atlanta and the fact that he played on his high school’s girls' volleyball team before co-ed sports were a thing, there is always a lot to unpack with Josh.

“Heavy is the head that wears the crown,” he likes to say. And as his friend and business partner, I believe in him. I believe in his vision, and in the person behind it. That’s why I wanted to do this with him. Sometimes it takes a little crazy to see a possibility other people miss.

People connect with people. That’s what made me want to build something with Josh, and it’s what I want JK Sportsbook to be about: more than just a place to track action. We have a real opportunity to build something with personality, curiosity, and room to grow.

We’re bringing back the internet. JK Sportsbook isn’t an app you download and forget about. I want it to be a place you choose to visit—a destination for sports coverage, ideas, and stories, the way people used to visit the sites that shaped how we consumed sports in the first place.

We’re here to ask questions, follow the stories, and shine a light on what we find.

That’s why I’m helping build JK Sportsbook.

— Corey Becker
VP of JK Sportsbook
